title: Foot Reflexology Chart Explained: Zones, Map and Evidence — cv.cm
description: A foot reflexology chart explained zone by zone: toes, ball, arch, heel and edges, left vs right foot, where the map comes from, and what research really shows.
h1: How do you read a foot reflexology chart?
answer: A foot reflexology chart is a traditional map that assigns parts of the body to areas of the feet: toes to the head, the ball to the chest, the arch to the digestive area, the heel to the lower back and pelvis, and the inner edge to the spine. It is a practice convention, not anatomy. Use it as a route for a relaxing foot session, never to judge symptoms.

body: Most charts follow the same broad logic. Picture a small person lying on the soles of both feet, head at the toes and pelvis at the heels. Each area of the sole is said to "reflect" the body part above it. The table below shows the common layout. Exact boundaries change from school to school.

body.note: This map comes from reflexology tradition. There is no known nerve, vessel or other anatomical path that connects a zone of the foot to the organ it is named after.

sections.h: Left foot, right foot, and why charts disagree
body: Charts treat the two feet as the two halves of the body. The right foot stands for the right side, so it carries the liver and gallbladder. The left foot stands for the left side, so it carries the heart area, the spleen and most of the stomach. Organs in the middle, such as the spine and bladder, appear on both feet along the inner edge.
If you compare charts from different books and countries, you will see differences:

ul: Some schools place the eyes and ears on the toe pads, others under the toes.
The size and position of the kidney, adrenal and intestine areas shift between charts.
Chinese foot massage traditions and Western reflexology use related but not identical maps, and many East Asian foot massage shops mix the two.
Hand and ear maps exist too, and they do not always match the foot map.

body: These differences are a useful reminder. The chart is a teaching convention that grew within schools of practice, not a measured map of the body. Pick one chart and use it as a route for your hands.

sections.h: Where reflexology comes from and what it claims
body: Foot pressure appears in many old traditions, including in Egypt, India and China. Modern Western reflexology has a clearer origin. In the early 1900s the American doctor William Fitzgerald described "zone therapy", which divided the body into ten vertical zones ending in the fingers and toes. In the 1930s the physiotherapist Eunice Ingham focused on the feet, drew detailed foot maps, and popularized the method now called reflexology.

Today, professional bodies describe it in modest terms. The UK Association of Reflexologists calls it a touch therapy based on the theory that points on the feet correspond to areas of the body, and it lists relaxation and well-being as its aims. Its guidance also says reflexologists should not diagnose, should not claim to treat a specific condition, and should not claim to cure anything.
So reflexology is a structured, pleasant way to massage the feet. It is not a way to find disease, and it does not replace medical care.

sections.h: A 10-minute relaxing foot session that follows the chart
body: You can use the chart simply as a route, so you cover the whole foot in an orderly way. Do this for yourself or for a family member or friend who is sitting or lying comfortably. Use a little lotion if the skin is dry. Time each step with a timer, for example cv.cm's countdown.

head: Step
Area
What to do
Time
rows: Hold the foot between both palms. Slide your hands from toes to ankle with light pressure.
Squeeze each toe pad gently between thumb and index finger. Make 3 small circles on each pad.
Thumb-walk across the ball in rows, left to right, then back.
Thumb-walk from the inner edge to the outer edge, row by row, moving down toward the heel.
Press the heel pad with the thumb or knuckles in slow circles. The heel can take firmer pressure.
Thumb-walk slowly from the heel up to the big toe joint along the bony edge.
Glide the thumb along the outer edge, then stroke the top of the foot from toes to ankle.
Hold the foot in both hands for a few breaths, then wrap it in a towel or sock.

body: Thumb walking is the main skill. Bend the top joint of the thumb a little, press, then straighten it slightly to inch forward a few millimeters. It looks like a caterpillar moving. Keep the other fingers wrapped around the top of the foot for support.
Do one foot, then the other. The whole session for both feet takes about 10 minutes if you keep each foot to 5.
Use words, not force, to set the level. On a 1 to 10 scale, aim for 3 to 5 on the arch and 4 to 6 on the heel.

ul: Light: the skin moves, the tissue below does not. Good for the top of the foot and for older or thin skin.
Medium: you feel the muscle and padding under the skin move. Good for most of the sole.
Firm: deeper, but still comfortable. Only on the heel and ball, and only if the person likes it.

body: Discomfort that feels good is fine. Sharp, burning or shooting pain means stop. A tender spot on the foot is usually a tender spot on the foot, such as a tight muscle, a callus or a strained heel. It is not a sign that the matching organ on the chart is unwell.

The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) says the idea that pressing points on the feet causes healing in other parts of the body has not been proven. A systematic review of 18 randomized trials by Edzard Ernst (2009) concluded that the best available evidence does not convincingly show that reflexology is an effective treatment for any medical condition. Most of the better-quality trials were negative, and many were small.

There are some narrower findings. NCCIH describes a study in women with advanced breast cancer that found improvement in some symptoms, such as shortness of breath, but not in others, such as nausea or pain. Cancer Research UK notes that studies of pain, sickness and anxiety have been small, with mixed results. It also says there is no scientific evidence that reflexology can cure or prevent any disease, but that many people use it to relax and cope with stress.

A fair summary: a gentle foot session may help you relax and feel cared for, much like other forms of massage. There is no good evidence that foot zones are linked to organs, that the chart can detect disease, or that it treats organ problems.

sections.h: Safety: when to skip it and when to see a doctor

body.note: Never use a reflexology chart to assess symptoms. Chest pain, trouble breathing, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw is an emergency. Call your local emergency number instead of rubbing the "heart area" of the foot.

body: Skip the session or keep it very gentle in these cases:

ul: Broken, infected or cracked skin, blisters, foot ulcers, or a fungal infection such as athlete's foot: do not massage that area.
A swollen, warm, red or painful calf, or a history of blood clots: do not massage the legs, and get medical help quickly if a calf is swollen and painful.
Diabetes or numb feet: check the skin first, use only light pressure, and stop if you see redness that lasts. People with numb feet cannot feel when pressure is too high.
Gout flare, a recent sprain, or a fresh bruise: avoid the area.
Bleeding disorders, blood thinners or a low platelet count: light pressure only.
Varicose veins on the feet or ankles: no deep pressure over them.
Pregnancy, cancer care or recent surgery: ask your midwife, doctor or care team first. Gentle touch is often fine in cancer care, but some areas may need to be avoided.

body: See a doctor or podiatrist if foot pain lasts more than a few weeks, if you have heel pain on your first steps every morning, if a toe or part of the foot changes color, or if a wound does not heal.

faq.q: What part of the foot is connected to the stomach?
faq.a: On most reflexology charts, the stomach area is the upper arch, mostly on the left foot, just below the ball of the foot. This is a traditional assignment, not an anatomical connection.

faq.q: Can a reflexologist tell what is wrong with you from your feet?
faq.a: No. There is no evidence that tender spots on the feet reveal disease in organs, and professional bodies say reflexologists should not diagnose. See a doctor for symptoms.

faq.q: Why does one spot on my foot hurt during reflexology?
faq.a: Usually because of something in the foot itself, such as a tight muscle, a callus, a strained plantar fascia or simply firm pressure. Ease the pressure, and see a doctor or podiatrist if the pain stays.

faq.q: Is reflexology the same as foot massage?
faq.a: Reflexology is a form of foot massage that follows a chart and uses thumb walking on set areas. A general foot massage uses kneading and stroking without a chart. Both are mainly ways to relax.

faq.q: How often can you do reflexology at home?
faq.a: A gentle 10-minute session once a day is fine for most healthy adults. If your feet feel sore the next day, halve the pressure and the time.
